e.etymology: A misspelling of Lawrence that shows up often enough in US records to count as a name. Lawrence comes from Latin Laurentius, 'man from Laurentum', a town near Rome, and was spread by St. Lawrence.
An 18th-century English coinage that joins Dora (Greek doron, 'gift') to the -inda ending of Belinda and Clarinda. George Farquhar used it in his 1707 comedy The Beaux' Stratagem.
An English surname from villages named Alford; the one in Lincolnshire is Old English for 'alder ford'. As a first name in the US it often overlapped with Alfred.
A spelling of Noreen, from Irish Nóirín, a pet form of Nóra. Nora began as a short form of Honora, from Latin honor.
An American form of Dorothea, from Greek doron, 'gift', and theos, 'god'. It was used mainly in the 1910s and 20s, alongside Dorothy and Dortha.
A spelling of Estelle, an Old French name from Latin stella, 'star'. In early US records this shorter spelling appears for boys as well as girls.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
A pet form of Dick, the medieval rhyming nickname for Richard (through Rick). Richard comes from Germanic ric, 'ruler', and hard, 'brave, strong'.
e.note: Dick is vulgar slang, so Dickie draws teasing; a dickie is also a false shirt front.

e.etymology: A spelling of Lakeisha, an African American name of the 1970s that adds the La- prefix to Keisha.

A misspelling of Geraldine found in US records. Geraldine is the feminine of Gerald, from Germanic ger, 'spear', and wald, 'rule'; a 16th-century poem about Lady Elizabeth FitzGerald, 'the fair Geraldine', launched it.
A spelling of Fern, from the English word for the plant, Old English fearn. Fern became a girls' name in the late 1800s, when plant and flower names were in fashion.
An African American name of the 1970s that joins the La- prefix to Shanda, itself a feminine form built on Shawn.
An African American name of the 1970s and 80s that joins the Sha- prefix to the -londa sound of Yolanda and Lalonda.
An American feminine name built on Bern-, as in Bernard (Germanic 'brave as a bear') and Bernice, with the Spanish-style ending -ita.
A spelling of Virgie, the pet form of Virginia. Virginia comes from the Roman family name Verginius and was long read as Latin virgo, 'maiden'.
A feminine form of Ron, the short form of Ronald, which is the Scottish form of Old Norse Rögnvaldr, from regin, 'counsel', and valdr, 'ruler'.
An elaboration of Flora or Florence with the -ene ending, used in the US in the early 1900s. Both go back to Latin flos, 'flower', and florens, 'flourishing'.
A transposed spelling of Brian that appears in US records from the years Brian was most popular. Brian is an old Irish name, probably from a Celtic root meaning 'hill' or 'high, noble'.
e.note: Reads as the English word brain, and will be said that way on sight.

e.etymology: A pet form of Oscar, Oswald and Osborn. Around 1900 it was also given to girls in the US.
namesakes: Ossie Davis (actor and civil rights activist)

e.etymology: A short form of Lucinda, an elaboration of Lucia, from Latin lux, 'light'. It has also been used as a variant of Cindy.
An African American name that peaked around 1990, built on the -esha sound of Aisha and Iesha with a Ty- opening.
A spelling of Denny, the pet form of Dennis, from Greek Dionysios, 'of Dionysus', the god of wine. St. Denis of Paris spread the name through medieval France and England.
A short form of Cleveland, an English surname and place name meaning 'land of cliffs' or 'hilly land', from Old English clif.
An African American name of the 1970s, formed with the Ta- prefix on the pattern of Tamika and Tanisha.
A spelling of Jean or Jeanne, from Old French Jehanne, the feminine of John (Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'). Marilyn Monroe was born Norma Jeane.
From an English surname and place name. As a first name in the American South it also served as a variant of Winfred.
An elaboration of Ethel with the -lyn ending. Ethel is a short form of Old English names such as Etheldred and Ethelinda, from aethel, 'noble'.
An American spelling of Deidra, a form of Deirdre, the tragic heroine of Irish legend. The meaning of Deirdre is not known.
A common misspelling of Sheila, the English form of Irish Síle, which is the Irish form of Cecilia. Cecilia comes from the Roman family name Caecilius, from Latin caecus, 'blind'.
A respelling of Mindy, the pet form of Melinda, an 18th-century English coinage that joins Mel-, as in Melissa (Greek meli, 'honey'), to the -inda ending of Belinda.
A pet form of Myrtle, from the evergreen shrub, Greek myrtos. Myrtle was one of the plant names that came into fashion for girls in the late 1800s.
